lines.text: Skincare is sold on claims, and almost nobody can tell whether it worked. Ninety percent of women say finding products that work is frustrating, and only fifteen percent think their wrinkle products work very well. So money is wasted on products that sit unused, and retailers only ever see the purchase, never the outcome. Willow measures that outcome, from ordinary phone photos, for the shopper and for the retailer that sold the product.

Meet Mei. She's twenty-six, lives in Singapore, and has acne along her cheeks, jaw and chin. Mei is simulated: her photos are generated, but every number you'll see was measured from them by Willow's live engine, exactly as it would be for you. Here are her eight Sundays, in five chapters.

Sunday evening, Mei takes three face photos by her window and a cheek close-up. Willow's engine on Cloud Run measures each one with classical computer vision, never with a language model, and this first check-in becomes her baseline. From now on, every reading is compared with her own skin and her own normal range, never with anyone else's. She also lists the products she uses. For her retailer, that's something it never had before: her goal and her whole routine, across brands.

lines.text: Week two: she starts a niacinamide serum and a centella cream. Her head was turned in that photo, so Willow doesn't compare it with her front-on baseline, and says so instead of guessing. Week three: she adds a retinol and a BHA, and her chin turns dry and flaky. She asks Wisp, Willow's Gemini adviser, and the routine check flags a retinoid and an acid on the same night. For the retailer, that's a clash caught early, before she gives up on both products or sends them back.

lines.text: Week four is her worst in ages: her period, a deadline at work, and little sleep. Her blemish count rises, but it stays inside her own normal range, so Willow doesn't call it a change. On Monday she stops the BHA, after Wisp flagged the clash, and by week five her skin feels calmer. A reading that can't be told apart from everyday noise never counts as a change. That honesty is what makes the outcome data worth trusting.

lines.text: Week six brings her first clear change: her blemishes are down, beyond her normal range. The marks from old spots are still there, so in week seven she adds a second niacinamide serum for them. The routine check notices she now has three products with niacinamide, and Is it working lines each product up with the reading it targets. For the retailer, that's the answer no single brand can see: which product in a mixed routine goes with a visible change.

Her cheek close-up couldn't be measured this time, and Willow says so. She asks Wisp whether she needs both niacinamide serums, and stops one. That's one less product to rebuy, and one more measured outcome for the retailer.

lines.text: So what did Mei gain? Proof instead of a feeling, with every reading measured against her own baseline. Problems caught in a week, not after a wasted month. Less money spent on products she didn't need. And advice in her own words, from an adviser that never invents a number.

And what does the retailer gain? Outcomes, not just purchases. With consent, and only in aggregate, check-ins like Mei's show what visibly works for each skin type and goal, across every brand on the shelf. That's how a retailer understands its customers, engages them, serves them better, and runs more efficiently, by stocking and promoting what's proven. That view is Proof by Willow.
Eight weeks later, here's Mei, measured against her own baseline. Open her account to explore the app yourself, open Proof by Willow for the retailer's side, or start your own baseline.

This is the other side of Willow: Proof, for brands and retailers. Today, a brand can say what a product is for, but not how often it visibly works, for whom, or how it compares on the shelf. Proof reads the check-ins people take in Willow, each against their own baseline, and shows what changed. The brand here is real, The Derma Co. The people are Willow's synthetic cohort, clearly labelled as simulated.

Chapter one: see what it does. Proof compares people who use a product with people who share their goals but don't use it. The difference is lift, and a product is Proven only when that lift stays above zero across its whole interval. That's evidence from real routines, not a lab claim or a star rating.

Chapter two: compare it fairly. Each product is ranked against others in its category that share a goal, all measured the same way. A brand sees exactly where it stands, and a retailer sees which products earn their place on the shelf.

Chapter three: who it works for. The same product doesn't work the same for everyone, so Proof splits every outcome by skin type and goal. A retailer can recommend each product where it works, and stop selling it to skin it doesn't suit, which is where returns come from.

Chapter four: an analyst that can't make things up. Gemini on Vertex AI works across Proof: it summarises, recommends, answers questions, drafts claims and sets up campaigns. It never measures. It only reads the aggregates Proof has already computed in BigQuery, and any number it writes that isn't in them is rejected before anyone sees it.

Chapter five: sell it on proof. Proof turns the measurements into claim-ready statements, and Gemini drafts copy from those statements only. Then only a Proven product can be promoted, only to the skin types and goals its evidence covers, and a random holdout never sees the card, so the lift a campaign causes is measured, not assumed.

So what does a retailer gain? It sells every product in a shopper's routine, so it's the one place that can see what actually works. Proof turns that into understanding customers, engaging them, serving them better, and running more efficiently, by stocking and promoting what's proven. And the shopper finds what works for her skin sooner.
